newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian government plans steps to ease VAT strain.
newsitem.headline: Croatian government plans steps to ease VAT strain.

text.p: Croatia's government is planning welfare measures and tax cuts next year to ease effects of a new value added tax (VAT) on poorer citizens, local newspaper Vjesnik reported on Tuesday.

It quoted Finance Minister Bozo Prka saying that as a result, average net wages could rise between eight and 10 percent to compensate for higher prices of goods such as foodstuffs, after the VAT is introduced at a rate of 22 percent.
This is expected to aggravate the already strenuous social situation in which many Croats, earning an average 2,000 kuna ($370), barely live above subsistence level.

But Prka told a panel discussion on VAT the non-taxable salary base would be raised and income tax reduced. Prka said the share of overheads, now at some 70 percent of gross wages, would be reduced, boosting net earnings to 55-60 percent of the total.

By helping the opening of new jobs, such measures are hoped to reduce unemployment and the share of grey market economy, estimated at 25 percent. They would result in an overall tax relief of some two billion kuna.

Prka ruled out the possibility of VAT sparking an inflationary boom because most prices, now taxed at a compounded rate of 26.5 percent imposed at various stages in production, would actually go down.
He cited clothing, footwear and most other consumables affecting family budgets as becoming cheaper.
Although prices of bread, milk, sugar and cooking oil are poised to rise, their increase would not be very pronounced because of an already incorporated "invisible" tax.

VAT is also designed to help exporters, who would get back the tax paid on all the inputs. This could make Croatian exports some 3-5 percent cheaper, the minister said. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
